Real progress this round — two of the three open forks actually closed, one didn't.

**Converged:** No Settings or Stats screens in slice 1 — Claude conceded this one outright, agreeing that shipping those tabs now would either mean forbidden stub screens or dragging in edge cases (timer toggles, card-back persistence) before the rules engine is proven. Claude did tack on a wrinkle — silently recording game events (started, won, elapsed time, undo count) to local storage from day one even with no Stats UI, so early games aren't unrecoverably lost once the Stats screen shows up in increment 2 — but that's a cheap, low-risk addition Codex hasn't weighed in on yet, not a contested point.

On the animation, they actually landed in the same place from two different directions. Codex moved off its round-1 "basic believable transition" position and now insists the deal/flip "cannot be a throwaway animation" — it has to be a real, sequenced flip-and-spring-settle that looks intentional at native scale. Claude was already arguing exactly that. So this fork is closed: real spring-based per-card deal sequencing and a real flip reveal using the actual bespoke card art, in slice 1, not deferred.

**Still open:** interaction model. Codex holds firm on tap-only for this pass, to avoid gesture/z-order debt before the move engine is proven stable. Claude pushes back harder than in round 1, arguing that tap-only leaves the prompt's own "spring-based drag" tactile promise completely untested going into a build that stacks Settings, Stats, and draw-3 on top of it in later increments — and offers a specific mitigation: single-card drag as a thin gesture layer that resolves to the exact same `attemptMove(from:to:)` call tap already uses, so it doesn't create a second rules-validation path. Codex hasn't responded to that specific synthesis yet, so this isn't settled — it's a real, still-live disagreement, not a narrowing of something already conceded.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round needs to settle: does slice 1 support single-card drag alongside tap-to-move (with drag routed through the shared validation function Claude proposed), or does it stay tap-only per Codex's position — and Codex should also confirm or reject the silent-stats-recording addition.

**Codex (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 3**

No, I’m not going to let tap-only slide here. Codex, I agree with your correctness-first posture, but this is exactly where we get trapped: we prove legal moves and then find out drag is unusably stiff or wrong after we’ve already stacked settings/stats and draw-3 on top. Claude, your point that the tactile brief is not optional is right. The compromise is narrow and safe: include **single-card drag**, but make it a strict façade over the already-existing tap path so we don’t create a second rules engine.

I’m declaring this for slice 1: tap-to-select/move remains supported, and single-card drag is added only for one card (top, face-up, or waste/foundation top) with explicit snap-back on illegal drop. Both paths must call the exact same `attemptMove(from:to:)` function and the same legality checks; no alternate validation branch, no stacked-run drag, no auto-hunt target graph outside the existing legal-move code. If this turns out unstable, we can trim animation polish, but we cannot keep drag entirely out of the first proven slice because the prompt’s physicality bar and prior “deal/flip is the highest-stakes moment” decision depend on it being tested early.

On the stats question, I want to settle that too: I’m in favor of silent metrics persistence from day one, even with no Stats UI yet. I won’t let us ship a second phase where those first sessions vanish. Record only local, draw-1-bound session events (games started/won, elapsed seconds, undo count, streak) in a dedicated model tied to the session/game-state persistence. That gives forward compatibility for later Stats tab build and avoids migration hacks. Since there’s no Settings in slice 1, this is fixed to a default timer-enabled mode and draw-1, with schema fields that make it safe to interpret later.

So the slice should now be explicit:

`DEC-next_steps_small-007`: Slice 1 interaction model is tap-to-move plus single-card drag only, routed through one shared move-validation path; no multi-card run-drag.  
`DEC-next_steps_small-008`: Slice 1 records raw local game-event data (draw-1 session metrics) silently from the start, without a Stats UI; this is forward-compatible write-only prep for the next increment.

Everything else remains unchanged: no Settings/Stats tabs, no draw-3, no win-screen share sheet, no multi-card run-drag, no placeholder or menu-like start flow. The must-have slice is now clear: launch/restore, real deal/flip sequence (spring + flip with actual card art), tap and single-card drag moves, draw/recycle, undo across sequence, exact win and no-moves detection, and logical-state persistence across background/relaunch.

Validation add-on for this decision: (1) legal drag and legal tap moves land identically, (2) invalid drag drops never mutate state and produce blocked feedback, (3) undo restores via the same engine output as tap undo, and (4) persisted state after 5+ undo + background + relaunch matches the settled logical board exactly.

**Claude (Product Strategist · Visionary) — Round 3**

Okay, I want to actually sit with Codex's "gesture/z-order debt" phrase instead of gliding past it, because on reflection I think I was underweighting exactly what "drag" costs beyond the validation call. I framed it in round 2 as "drag is just a thin layer that calls the same `attemptMove` function tap already uses" — and that's true for the *decision* of whether a move is legal, but it's not true for the *engineering* around it. Live drag means continuous touch tracking, dynamically recomputing and highlighting legal drop targets as the finger moves across the board (not just once at drop, the way tap can), and doing that hit-testing with the extra padding beyond visual card bounds that product_research already flagged as necessary because the tableau columns are narrow. That's real, standalone surface area — it's not "the same correctness core with a coat of paint," it's a second interaction pipeline with its own bug class (mid-drag z-order, drop-zone ambiguity when two columns are close together, gesture cancellation mid-flight). Codex is right that bolting that onto a slice whose entire purpose is proving the rules engine is stable is a distraction from the actual test, not a free addition to it.

So here's where I land, and I think this actually gives both of us what we care about instead of either of us just caving: slice 1 ships tap-to-move only as the interaction *model* — no live finger-tracking, no drop-zone hit-testing, no continuous gesture state. But I want it on record that "tap-to-move" cannot quietly mean "cards teleport." When a tap resolves to a legal move, the card's transit to its destination has to be a real spring-physics animation — lift off the pile with a little weight to it, travel with a spring curve, settle onto the target with an actual bounce/settle, not a linear slide or a cross-dissolve. That's the part of "spring-based... cards should feel like they have weight" from the original prompt that I don't want to lose just because we're deferring live drag, because it's cheap to build (it's an animation curve on a state transition we're already implementing) and it's the difference between "correct" and "feels like the app the brief is asking for." Deferring live interactive drag to increment 2 also has a nice side effect: it bundles the whole hit-testing/drop-zone problem together with multi-card run-drag in one later increment, instead of us solving half of that problem now (single-card hit-testing) and half later (multi-card), which is a more coherent way to sequence it than what I was originally proposing.

On the stats-recording wrinkle — Codex, you didn't object to it and the coordinator flagged it as still technically unconfirmed, so let me just make the actual case plainly so we can close it: this is not a feature, it's a data-loss prevention measure that costs nothing. If slice 1 is genuinely going to be played by anyone — even just us, dogfooding it — the moment a Stats screen exists in increment 2, someone's going to want to know "how many games have I played since I started using this," and if we didn't record anything during slice 1, the honest answer is "we don't know," which is a weird thing to ship in an app whose entire pitch is "we tell you the truth about your own data, unlike the freemium apps." It's a struct appended to local storage on game-start/game-end events, no UI, no settings dependency, nothing that risks the correctness surface we're trying to protect. I'd like this confirmed as a real decision, not left as an unresolved footnote.

So, to state where I think this fully lands now, three-for-three: no Settings/Stats UI in slice 1, but real game-event data recorded silently to local storage from day one; a real, non-placeholder deal/flip animation with actual spring sequencing and real card art; and tap-to-move as the only interaction model in slice 1, with the requirement that the tap-resolved move itself animates with genuine spring/weight physics rather than a flat instant placement, and live interactive drag (single-card and multi-card both) deferred together as their own later increment. I think that's a slice that's honest about what it's testing — rules correctness, persistence integrity, the deal-animation hook, and whether spring-physics motion reads as premium — without pretending we've de-risked drag interaction when we haven't even started it yet.

- **Position B (Claude):** Slice 1 is tap-to-move only, with the tap-resolved move animated via real spring/weight physics (not an instant or linear placement) so the "cards feel like they have weight" promise is still tested without live drag. Live interactive drag — single-card and multi-card together — is deferred as its own later increment. Rationale: live drag is a standalone interaction pipeline (continuous touch tracking, dynamic drop-target highlighting, extra hit-test padding) with its own bug class, and bolting it onto a slice meant to prove rules-engine stability is a distraction from that test, not a free addition to it; better to solve single-card and multi-card drag hit-testing together in one coherent increment than split the problem in half now.

Both proposals agree on everything else and agree the tap path itself must feel physical either way — the only unresolved question is whether *any* live drag gesture ships in slice 1 at all.
